props.title: Broken Blossoms
props.initialSlug: Tragic love between Chinese man and abused girl

sections.content: Broken Blossoms (1919) stands as D.W. Griffith's most intimate masterpiece, a haunting portrait of cross-cultural love in London's gritty Limehouse district. After the epic scope of Birth of a Nation (1915) and Intolerance (1916), Griffith stripped everything down to raw emotion. Lillian Gish delivers one of silent cinema's most devastating performances as Lucy, an abused teenager who finds tender care from a Chinese immigrant (Richard Barthelmess). The famous "closet scene" where Lucy frantically spins as her father tries to break down the door remains a masterclass in building tension through performance and editing.

sections.content: While problematic in its yellowface casting of Barthelmess as "The Yellow Man," Broken Blossoms attempted unprecedented sympathy toward interracial relationships for its era. The film's intimate scale influenced later chamber dramas like Sunrise: A Song of Two Humans (1927) and The Passion of Joan of Arc (1928). Griffith's atmospheric use of fog and shadows in the Limehouse sets would impact film noir decades later. SUBHEAD: Technical Innovation and Visual Poetry

Griffith's innovative close-ups and iris effects create a dreamy, poetic atmosphere that was revolutionary for 1919. The film's visual motifs - particularly the recurring broken flower imagery - demonstrate sophisticated symbolic storytelling that influenced European impressionist cinema like The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari (1920) and The Last Laugh (1924). The intimate lighting techniques developed by cinematographer Billy Bitzer would become standard practice in Hollywood.
